clue.text: Like Tristram Shandy, she had an uncle toby

definitions.text: Like Tristram Shandy, she had an uncle toby

parts.words: Like Tristram Shandy, she had an uncle toby
parts.note: Sterne's hero has an Uncle Toby; the Shakespeare heroine wanted here has an uncle called Sir Toby Belch

explanation.surface: A reader notices that a heroine shares a family quirk with Sterne's narrator.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night the countess's household includes her uncle Sir Toby Belch, matching Tristram Shandy's Uncle Toby.
explanation.definitionFit: The countess of Twelfth Night is niece to Sir Toby Belch, just as Tristram is nephew to Toby Shandy.

clue.text: Girl at garden party, coming from chap's meadow ()

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Girl at garden party, coming from chap's meadow () (5)': the empty brackets show a word lost in OCR, and no reading of 'chap's meadow' gives the letters; only the Mansfield definition is sound.
annotationWithheld.clue: Girl at garden party, coming from chap's meadow ()

clue.text: Poor service in Virginia in back-to front book

indicators.note: the shuffled letters sit inside the abbreviation, so 'in' signals a container

parts.note: VA is the standard abbreviation for the US state of Virginia

indicators.note: poor work is badly done, so the word that follows is rearranged

explanation.surface: Bad service in a Virginia bookshop where the volume is printed the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges SERVICE into ICEVERS, which goes between V and A. Vice Versa is F. Anstey's novel in which father and son swap bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: Vice Versa, the Anstey novel, is a book whose title means the other way round.

clue.text: Rugby prop raised poetic issue

parts.note: a pillar of Rugby School, its headmaster, fathered a son who became a poet

explanation.surface: A rugby forward lifts his teammate while arguing about poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arnold was the famous headmaster of Rugby School and father of the poet Matthew Arnold; 'prop' and 'issue' mean support and offspring, not a rugby player and a question.
explanation.definitionFit: The family name is shared by the reforming Rugby headmaster and his son, a Victorian poet.

clue.text: Hypocrite's intimate address in French conceals art and very loud English

indicators.note: the French pronoun hides the next word inside it, so 'conceals' signals a container

parts.note: tu is the familiar French word for 'you'
taken as written
ff (fortissimo) is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A two-faced Frenchman's familiar manner masks some art and very loud English.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'Hypocrite's' stands for 'is'. Molière's play is named for its pious hypocrite.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière's title character is the model of the religious hypocrite, his name now a byword for sanctimony.

clue.text: Fitzgerald's indelible writer adopted by A. Christie

definitions.text: Fitzgerald's indelible writer adopted by A. Christie

parts.words: Fitzgerald's indelible writer adopted by A. Christie
parts.note: Edward FitzGerald's Rubaiyat speaks of a hand that writes and cannot be erased, and Agatha Christie used the phrase as a title

explanation.surface: A writer whose ink cannot be erased is taken on by a crime novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam: 'The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, Moves on'. Christie took the phrase for a Miss Marple novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rubaiyat's image of fate as a writing hand gave Christie the title of a 1942 mystery.

clue.text: Lear's ass oddly revealed in didactic romance

indicators.note: arranged oddly means put in a strange order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name with its possessive S, all letters used

explanation.surface: Edward Lear's donkey turns up strangely in a moralising tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges LEARSASS. Samuel Johnson's Rasselas is a philosophical tale of an Abyssinian prince.
explanation.definitionFit: Johnson's Rasselas is a moral fable in prose romance form, written to teach about the search for happiness.

clue.text: Canterbury Tales murderer, from the bountiful riches of Byron

indicators.note: the name is taken out of the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A Chaucerian killer draws on the lavish riches of Byron's verse.
explanation.walkthrough: Not Chaucer: the Lee sisters' Canterbury Tales include 'Kruitzner', where Ulric is the murderer, and Byron's drama Werner retells it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Lee sisters' tale, retold by Byron, the son of Kruitzner secretly commits the murder.

clue.text: More of them needed to accommodate a novel suggestion of Waugh

definitions.text: More of them needed to accommodate a novel suggestion of Waugh

parts.words: More of them needed to accommodate a novel suggestion of Waugh
parts.note: Waugh's novel title Put Out More Flags would need more poles to fly them on

explanation.surface: Someone works out what extra equipment Evelyn Waugh's advice would require.
explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn Waugh's 1942 novel is Put Out More Flags; more flags would need more of these to hang from.
explanation.definitionFit: Masts for flying banners would be needed in greater numbers to put out more flags.

clue.text: Meat-smoking characters from pirate edition?

parts.note: the word for these sea-robbers comes from the boucan, a frame for smoking meat, and Edith Wharton used it as a title

explanation.surface: A query about some cooks found in an unauthorised printing of a book.
explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from French boucanier, one who smokes meat on a boucan; Edith Wharton's last novel is The Buccaneers.
explanation.definitionFit: Caribbean pirates took their name from the meat-curing hunters of Hispaniola.

clue.text: Study critic: discover poet

definitions.meaning: to study a text is to go through it
Herbert ... was an English art critic
Herbert ... was also a war poet

explanation.surface: An instruction to look into a critic and uncover a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Herbert Read was both art critic and poet; 'discover' links the senses.
explanation.definitionFit: To pore over a book is the verb; Sir Herbert, critic and poet, carries the surname.

clue.text: He apparently received the order of the garter from 1 Across

definitions.text: He apparently received the order of the garter from 1 Across

parts.words: He apparently received the order of the garter from 1 Across
parts.note: the forged letter seemingly from the countess commands its reader to wear yellow stockings cross-gartered

explanation.surface: A man seems to have been knighted by a lady.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night Maria forges a letter in Olivia's hand telling the steward to go cross-gartered; 'order of the garter' is an instruction, not the knighthood.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivia's steward obeys the forged letter's command to wear cross-garters.

clue.text: "The Legion of Honour has been conferred upon me. However, few —— that distinction." (Mark Twain)

definitions.text: "The Legion of Honour has been conferred upon me. However, few —— that distinction." (Mark Twain)

parts.words: "The Legion of Honour has been conferred upon me. However, few —— that distinction." (Mark Twain)
parts.note: the gap takes the verb meaning to avoid, so Twain says the French honour is so common few avoid it

explanation.surface: Mark Twain jokes that the French award is handed to nearly everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in: Twain's quip is that the Legion of Honour is so widely given that few avoid getting it.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to get away from, completing Twain's quip about an over-awarded honour.

clue.text: Old sailor at start of reading by Wyndham Lewis

parts.note: tar is an old word for a sailor

indicators.note: only the first letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: A veteran seaman begins a reading of Wyndham Lewis's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the novel: Tarr (1918) is by Wyndham Lewis.
explanation.definitionFit: Wyndham Lewis's first novel, about artists in Paris, bears this title.

clue.text: Lawrentian flute symbolically broken

parts.note: in a D. H. Lawrence novel the hero's flute is smashed, a symbol of his broken life

explanation.surface: A D. H. Lawrence musical instrument is smashed with meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: Aaron Sisson in D. H. Lawrence's novel plays the flute, his biblically named rod, which is broken at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Lawrence's novel names the hero's flute after the staff that blossomed in Exodus.

clue.text: Greyish-yellow Walpole heroine

definitions.meaning: a pale buff colour, named in English after a Spanish princess
the heroine of Horace Walpole's Gothic novel The Castle of Otranto

explanation.surface: A sallow-faced heroine from a Gothic novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour name and the Otranto heroine pursued by Manfred share one name.

clue.text: Effort concealed by Morse code

definitions.meaning: Inspector Morse kept his first name secret for years

explanation.surface: A struggle to hide something in dots and dashes.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Dexter's Inspector Morse hid his first name until late in the series.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt or striving is the noun, and Morse's long-hidden first name is the same word.

clue.text: Note, revolutionary allowed French historian

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
Che Guevara, the Marxist revolutionary
let means allowed

explanation.surface: A remark that a rebel had been permitted to write French history.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Michelet wrote a many-volume history of France and of the Revolution.

clue.text: It must have been a strain for John Masters

definitions.text: It must have been a strain for John Masters

parts.words: It must have been a strain for John Masters
parts.note: the clue completes a John Masters title, with the missing word placed before Strain

explanation.surface: Sympathy for a novelist who must have found the work hard going.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masters wrote a novel called The Breaking Strain; the answer is the word before 'Strain'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word that goes before Strain in the Masters title also means snapping under pressure.

clue.text: Beach wrote of it on the sea

definitions.text: Beach wrote of it on the sea

parts.words: Beach wrote of it on the sea
parts.note: Edward L. Beach's submarine novel is titled with something lying on the sea

explanation.surface: Seaside lines written about something floating on the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: Beach is the author Edward L. Beach, whose novel is Dust on the Sea, not a seashore.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine powdery particles are what Edward Beach's title places on the sea.

clue.text: Flying instructor to Brutus

parts.note: one of Brutus's men in Julius Caesar urges him to flee at Philippi

explanation.surface: A man who taught a Roman to pilot an aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, at Philippi, Clitus cries 'Fly, my lord, fly', so he instructs Brutus to flee, not to pilot.
explanation.definitionFit: Brutus's follower at Philippi tells him to flee from the battlefield.

clue.text: A rough sort of rhyme is quite sufficient

explanation.surface: A crude rhyme will do perfectly well.
explanation.definitionFit: The word ends with the same sound as rough and means adequate.

clue.text: Posh daughter wholly represents early dramatist

parts.note: U means upper-class, as in Nancy Mitford's U and non-U
all means wholly

explanation.surface: A well-bred girl fully acts out an old play.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Udall wrote Ralph Roister Doister, one of the first English comedies.

clue.text: Edit fall (characters might be doomed anyway)

indicators.note: the letters may be put down any way, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A note that letters falling about spell disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anyway' tells you to rearrange EDITFALL; the words 'characters might be' name the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doomed and star-crossed both mean destined for misfortune.

clue.text: ". . suddenly the wheels stood still, / And a voice cried 'in my ear!" (Longfellow) ()

definitions.text: ". . suddenly the wheels stood still, / And a voice cried 'in my ear!" (Longfellow)

parts.words: ". . suddenly the wheels stood still, / And a voice cried 'in my ear!" (Longfellow)
parts.note: the gap in the Longfellow line takes the name of the girl in The Golden Legend

explanation.surface: Longfellow's lines in which a voice calls out a name.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in from Longfellow's The Golden Legend, whose heroine is the peasant girl who offers her life for Prince Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of the girl in Longfellow's Golden Legend fills the gap in the line.

clue.text: Terminal offering, possibly by fat lady

definitions.text: Terminal offering, possibly by fat lady

parts.words: Terminal offering, possibly by fat lady
parts.note: the saying goes that it is not over till the fat lady sings, so the final piece is her song

explanation.surface: Something on offer at an airport, maybe from a heavy woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It ain't over till the fat lady sings': her solo at an opera's end is the final offering. 'Terminal' is not an airport.
explanation.definitionFit: An operatic solo song is what the soprano sings to end the show.

clue.text: Objective of Woolf's work

parts.note: Virginia Woolf's novel title begins with To, naming a destination

explanation.surface: A critic asks what Woolf was aiming at in her writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf's novel To the Lighthouse names its goal: the trip out to the light.
explanation.definitionFit: The trip planned throughout Woolf's novel aims at a coastal beacon tower.

clue.text: Devotee uses artificial language subsequently

parts.note: Ido is a constructed language derived from Esperanto
later means subsequently

explanation.surface: A fan who speaks an invented language afterwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An idol-worshipper is an ardent worshipper, so a devotee.

clue.text: John Masefield's was accepted as up-to date in

definitions.text: John Masefield's was accepted as up-to date in

parts.words: John Masefield's was accepted as up-to date in
parts.note: Masefield's novel The ___ of To-day: its title thoroughfare is the up-to-date one

explanation.surface: A remark that Masefield's work was thought modern.
explanation.walkthrough: John Masefield wrote the novel The Street of To-day (1911).
explanation.definitionFit: A town road is named in Masefield's title as belonging to today.
